title: A Man In Michigan Used A Rock To Prop His Door Open For 30 Years. It Was A Meteorite Worth $100,000 - Futura-Sciences
excerpt: The farmer who sold him the land told him exactly what it was. It took three decades, and a news story about space rocks, for anyone to check.
content:
The farmer who sold him the land told him exactly what it was. It took three decades, and a news story about space rocks, for anyone to check.

In 1988, a man from Grand Rapids bought a farm in Edmore, a small town in central Michigan about 30 miles southwest of Mount Pleasant. While the farmer was showing him around, they walked out to a shed. A large, odd-looking rock was holding the door open.

The buyer asked what it was. A meteorite, the farmer said, as if it were nothing. It had come down on the property in the 1930s, and according to the farmer, it made a heck of a noise when it hit. It was part of the property, he added, so the new owner could have it.

Thirty years as a doorstop

For the next three decades it did the job it had always done: it propped a door open. Now and then, his children took it to school for show-and-tell.

In early 2018, he read news reports about people in Michigan selling fragments of a meteorite that had fallen in the state that January for thousands of dollars. He started to wonder what his own rock was worth, and decided to have it examined at Central Michigan University.

“Meteor wrongs”

The rock landed on the desk of Mona Sirbescu, a geology professor who had spent 18 years fielding the same request from the public. People bring in stones they are sure came from space. For 18 years, her answer had been categorically no. She had a name for them: meteor wrongs.

This time, when the man pulled the rock out of a bag, she could tell immediately that it was different. Analysis showed it was an iron meteorite, made of about 88.5 percent iron and 11.5 percent nickel, the metal alloy typical of fragments from the cores of shattered asteroids. It weighed a little over 22 pounds, about 10 kilograms. To be sure, a slice was sent to the Smithsonian Institution in Washington, which confirmed the identification.

It was the sixth-largest meteorite ever recorded in Michigan. Central Michigan University put its potential value at around $100,000. Sirbescu described it as the most valuable specimen she had ever held, both in money and in scientific terms.

Why an ugly rock is worth so much

Iron meteorites are pieces of the metallic cores of small planetary bodies that formed in the early solar system, melted, separated into layers, and were later broken apart by collisions. They are among the few samples humans can hold of what the inside of a planet looks like. Unlike stony meteorites, which can resemble ordinary rocks, irons are heavy for their size, often magnetic and resistant to weathering, which is why one can survive decades on a farm floor.

Their value comes from rarity and demand. Museums, universities and private collectors compete for large specimens, especially when the fall location is documented. A heavy iron with a known history and a confirmed classification is worth far more than its weight in metal.

The owner said he intended to give part of the proceeds from any sale to the university. The meteorite came to be known by the name of the town where it had held the shed door open: Edmore.

Check the doorstop

The story has a close cousin in Romania, where a woman propped her door open for decades with what turned out to be one of the largest pieces of amber of its kind. In Australia, a man kept a rock for years hoping it contained gold, and it turned out to be a meteorite older than the Earth.

Sirbescu’s 18 years of “no” are the other half of the lesson. Most rocks people suspect of coming from space are ordinary slag, iron ore or concretions. What made the Edmore rock different was not how it looked, but that someone had seen it fall and passed the story on with it.
